For some reason, bad guys frequently have British accents in American film and television.

I have some theories as to why that is.

I think it has a lot to do with how Hollywood markets to the US first. A requisite feature of the bad guy seems to be that he's easy to distinguish from everyone else. Given this, you don't want your bad guy to sound like everyone else you're marketing to. This is usually most easily accomplished by making them sound or look different. In the case of Englishmen, the western world has come to associate the accent with calculating intelligence, smooth moves, and sharp wit. We can probably blame decades of James Bond for that. Englishmen are thought to be well spoken and articulated, but also as having a bit of a superiority complex. This makes for a great villain blend that people tend to find interesting.

Of course, you won't just see Englishmen in that role - you'll often seen Germans, Russians, and other non-Americans as well, since the stereotypes associated with those cultures tend to prevail with movie characters. Just like Italian accents are almost always associated with pasta and the mob, and Chinese accents are associated with Kung-Fu and mysticism.

In any case, we love the British actors. I'm always a bit surprised when I see an interview where a person is out of character speaking with a British accent, and the last movie I saw them in they had a completely neutral American accent. I often wonder how difficult it is for them to turn it off and on like that.

Accents can be learned and turning it on and off is more about what you're saying and having learned the timing and intonation. Some are better at it than others and have an ear for the accent but it is easier to work with a native speaker and repeat what they say and have them critique it. There are also phrases which are a dead give away, and others which are seriously never used but associated with the accent (ooh, I do say missus.)
